subject: mathematics
question_text: Prove that in any triangle the altitudes are concurrent.

mark_split.label: Set up the triangle and name the meeting point
Take that point as the origin
Read off the third altitude and conclude

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IA (2026-27 edition), book p.79, chapter 7 PRODUCT OF VECTORS, Long Answer question 10. Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the Mathematics-IA volume prints no per-step mark allocation on any answer. The 1+1+2+2+1+1 split gives two marks to each of the two perpendicularity conditions, because writing them as dot products is the whole method, and keeps single marks for the set-up, the addition and the conclusion. Paper position: Maths-1A Section C prints 3 long answers at 8 marks each and the student answers any 2; Product of Vectors is one of the units that can fill a Section-C slot. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove that the three altitudes of a triangle meet at one point.

steps.label: Set up the triangle
steps.margin_note: First mark. Two of the three altitudes are taken first, and the proof shows the third passes through where they cross. Saying why those two must cross is part of the mark.
steps.memory_tip: Start with TWO altitudes, not three. The third is what the proof produces.
lines: Let ABC be a triangle. An altitude is
the line through a vertex at right
angles to the opposite side. All three
lie in the plane of the triangle.
BC and CA are not parallel, so the
altitude through A and the altitude
through B are not parallel and must
meet. Let them meet at O.

recall.must_convey: That two of the altitudes must cross, because the sides they are at right angles to are not parallel, and that their meeting point is called O.
accept: take the altitudes through A and B, they are not parallel so they meet at a point O
two altitudes must cross because BC and CA are not parallel
call the point where two altitudes meet O
rendu altitudes kalustai, aa point ni O ani rasta
start with two altitudes and name their meeting point

steps.why: Concurrency is always proved this way: take the point where two of the lines cross and show the third passes through it. Assuming all three meet would assume the result.
common_mistakes: Assuming all three altitudes already meet, which is the thing being proved.
Defining the altitude as the line to the midpoint, which is the median.

steps.label: Take O as the origin
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Placing the origin at O is what makes OA simply a, with no subtraction. Every dot product below stays short because of this one choice.
steps.memory_tip: Put the origin at O, and then OA is just a — no subtraction anywhere.
lines: Take O as the origin and let a, b, c be
the position vectors of A, B, C.
Then OA = a, OB = b, OC = c and
BC = c − b, CA = a − c, BA = a − b.

recall.must_convey: That O is taken as the origin, so the position vectors of A, B, C are a, b, c and the sides are their differences.
accept: take O as the origin so OA is a, OB is b and OC is c
with O at the origin the sides are c minus b, a minus c and a minus b
put the origin at the meeting point
O ni origin ga theeskunte OA ante a matrame
let a b c be the position vectors from O

steps.why: The origin can be placed anywhere, and placing it at O removes every subtraction from the vectors along the altitudes. That is what keeps the algebra to three short lines.
common_mistakes: Taking A as the origin, which leaves OA as a difference and lengthens every line.
Writing BC as b − c, which is the vector from C to B.

steps.label: First altitude
steps.margin_note: Two marks. O lies on the altitude through A, so the line OA is at right angles to BC. Written as a dot product and expanded, this is equation (1).
steps.memory_tip: O is on the altitude through A, so OA is at right angles to BC.
lines: O lies on the altitude through A, so
OA ⊥ BC :

recall.must_convey: That O lying on the altitude through A means a·(c − b) = 0, which expands to a·c − a·b = 0.
accept: O is on the altitude through A so a dot c minus b is zero
that expands to a dot c minus a dot b equals zero
OA is at right angles to BC
a dot c minus b zero, expand cheste a dot c minus a dot b
the first condition is a dot c equals a dot b

steps.why: A right angle between two vectors is exactly a zero dot product. Expanding it separates the products so that the two conditions can be added later.
common_mistakes: Pairing A with a side through A instead of the opposite side BC.
Using a × (c − b) = 0, which says parallel and not at right angles.

steps.label: Second altitude
steps.margin_note: Two marks. The same statement for B, with the letters moved on one place. Note that b·a is written as a·b so the two equations can be added.
steps.memory_tip: The same statement with the letters moved on one place: A to B, BC to CA.
lines: O lies on the altitude through B, so
OB ⊥ CA :

recall.must_convey: That O lying on the altitude through B means b·(a − c) = 0, which expands to a·b − b·c = 0.
accept: O is on the altitude through B so b dot a minus c is zero
that gives a dot b minus b dot c equals zero
OB is at right angles to CA
rendo condition a dot b minus b dot c zero
the second condition is a dot b equals b dot c

steps.why: A dot product does not change when its two vectors are swapped, so b·a can be written as a·b. That is what makes the two equations line up for adding.
common_mistakes: Leaving the term as b·a, so the cancellation in the next step is not visible.
Pairing B with BC instead of with the opposite side CA.

steps.label: Add the two conditions
steps.margin_note: Seventh mark. The a·b terms have opposite signs, so they cancel when the two equations are added. What is left involves only b, c and a.
steps.memory_tip: The a·b terms carry opposite signs, so adding removes them.
lines: Adding (1) and (2), the a·b terms cancel:
a·c − b·c = 0

recall.must_convey: That adding (1) and (2) cancels the a·b terms and leaves a·c − b·c = 0, that is (a − b)·c = 0.
accept: add the two equations, a dot b cancels and a dot c minus b dot c is left
the sum gives a minus b dotted with c equals zero
the middle terms cancel because their signs are opposite
rendu add cheste a dot b cancel avthundi
we are left with a minus b dot c equals zero
heard_as: a dot c minus b dot c

steps.why: The two conditions were written in the same letters on purpose. Adding them removes the shared term and leaves exactly the third condition.
common_mistakes: Subtracting the two equations, which leaves a·c + b·c − 2a·b and no third condition.
Thinking the a·b terms add rather than cancel, and being left with 2a·b.

steps.label: The third altitude
steps.margin_note: Last mark. (a − b) is BA, so this says OC is at right angles to AB. That is exactly the altitude through C, and O is on it.
steps.memory_tip: a − b is BA, so the result says OC is at right angles to AB.
lines: Now a − b = BA, so c·BA = 0, that is
OC ⊥ AB.
So O lies on the line through C at right
angles to AB, which is the third altitude.

lines.text: The three altitudes meet at O.

recall.must_convey: That (a − b) is BA, so OC is at right angles to AB, which puts O on the third altitude and proves the three are concurrent.
accept: a minus b is BA so OC is at right angles to AB, the third altitude
O lies on all three altitudes so they are concurrent
the third altitude also passes through O
moodava altitude kuda O gunda velthundi
hence the three altitudes meet at one point

steps.why: The algebra finishes one line before the proof does. Naming a − b as BA is what turns the dot product back into a statement about altitudes.
common_mistakes: Stopping at (a − b)·c = 0 without saying what it means.
Naming the point of concurrence without saying the third altitude passes through it.
